title: the Purusha Sukta
hook: "the moon was born from his mind." the Purusha Sukta turns the parts of a body into the sky, the wind and the earth

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Purusha Sukta's hardest verse: mouth, arms, thighs and feet as four groups, and the honest argument over what that means. Whose unthanked work did you notice? Day one thousand two hundred sixty.

The moon was born from his mind. That's a line from the Purusha Sukta, in paraphrase, and it comes with a whole list. The sun, from his eye. The wind, from his breath. The sky, from his head. Look up some clear night and try reading the sky that way: not as a ceiling, but as a face, a breath, a mind, all far bigger than yours, and all somehow related to yours. The hymn has turned from the people of the world to the world itself, and it draws the map using a body. Today: the sky made from a person.
screen: `THE MOON, FROM HIS MIND.` → `THE SUN, FROM HIS EYE.` → `A SKY MADE FROM A PERSON.`

segments.voice: Verse thirteen, in Sanskrit, begins chandrama manaso jatah: the moon, born from mind. From his eye, the sun was born. From his mouth, Indra and Agni, the god of storm and the god of fire. From his breath, Vayu, the wind. Verse fourteen goes on. From his navel, the middle air. From his head, the sky took shape. From his feet, the earth. From his ear, the directions. And so, it says, they fashioned the worlds. Listen to how well the pairs fit. Eye and sun: both have to do with light and seeing. Breath and wind: the same moving air, small and large. Feet and earth: what stands, and what is stood on. Ear and the directions: sound comes from every side. Mind and moon is harder. Some readers hear the moon's waxing and waning as a picture of a mind that changes, but the verse only sets the two side by side. Earlier on this path, the Aitareya Upanishad told the same story in reverse: fire became speech and entered the mouth, wind became breath and entered the nose, the sun became sight and entered the eyes, the moon became mind. Hymn and Upanishad together make a loop. The world comes out of a person; and the world's powers come back to live in a person. This week has moved from the Nasadiya's cord and its open ending into the Purusha: a thousand heads, the quarter we can see, the great offering, the hard verse about the body's parts, and now the sky. Each day, the same idea from a new side: one person, and everything.
screen: `MIND TO MOON, EYE TO SUN.` · `BREATH TO WIND, FEET TO EARTH.` · `THE AITAREYA: THE SAME, IN REVERSE.` · `ONE PERSON, AND EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let the body and the sky meet. Settle, and breathe. Feel the breath at the nostrils, and let it be wind for a moment, the same air that moves the trees. Notice light through your closed eyelids, and let it be the sun. Feel the feet on the floor, and let the floor be the earth. Listen for sounds from every side, the directions. Then rest the mind, and let it be as quiet as the moon. Go slowly. Body, then world, then body again. If you pray, you can pray there. The bell holds the time.
The Purusha Sukta. In verses thirteen and fourteen, mind becomes the moon, eye the sun, breath the wind, feet the earth, and so the worlds are fashioned. Today's word.
Your line: the Purusha Sukta. Today, step outside once and match one thing in the sky, the sun, a cloud, the wind, to something in you. A week on the hill, done. Day one thousand two hundred sixty.

howItsDone: The Purusha Sukta is recited in Hindu worship and Vedic chanting, and its picture of the world fashioned from the cosmic person's body is echoed in later texts such as the Aitareya Upanishad.

fork.setup: you're the poet, mapping the sky onto a body. what do you say the earth came from?
fork.reveal: verse fourteen: from his feet, the earth. from his head, the sky; from his navel, the middle air.

original.note: Sanskrit: the moon was born from mind. The opening of Rig Veda 10.90.13.

trapdoor: what you thought: the hymn just says a god made the sun and moon.
what it means: the sun, moon, wind, sky and earth come from the parts of the cosmic person: eye, mind, breath, head and feet.
what a scholar hears: chandrama manaso jatash chakshoh suryo ajayata, and the Aitareya Upanishad running the same map backwards, from the world into the body.

sources.ref: Rig Veda 10.90.13–14 (from his eye the sun, from his mouth Indra and Agni, from his breath the wind; from his navel the middle air, from his head the sky, from his feet the earth, from his ear the directions; so they fashioned the worlds)
Aitareya Upanishad 1.2.4 (fire became speech and entered the mouth; wind became breath and entered the nostrils; the sun became sight and entered the eyes; the moon became mind and entered the heart)
